source_text: Vae, ait, per quem traditur filius hominis. ergo iam \'uae* constat imprecationis et comminationis inclamationem intellegendam et irato et offenso deputandam, nisi si ludas impune erat tantum sceleris relaturus. at si impune, uacat \'uae\'; si non impune, utique ab eo puniendus, in quem scelus traditionis admisit. porro si sciens passus est hominem, quem ipse comitatui suo adsciuerat, in tantum scelus ruere, noli iam de creatore circa Adam retractare quae in tuum quoque deum retorquentur: aut ignorasse illum, qui non ex prouidentia obstitit peccaturo, aut obsistere non potuisse, si (non) ignorabat, aut noluisse, si et sciebat et poterat, atque ita malitiosum iudicandum, qui passus sit hominem suum ex delicto perire. suadeo igitur agnoscas potius et in isto creatorem quam parem illi deum optimum aduersus sententiam tuam facias. nam et Petrum praesumptorie aliquid elocutum negationi potius destinando zeloten deum tibi ostendit. debuit etiam osculo tradi, propheticus scilicet Christus, ut eius scilicet filius, qui labiis a populo diligebatur. Perductus in consessum, an ipse esset Christus, interrogatur. de quo Christo Iudaei quaesissent nisi de suo? cur ergo non uel tunc alium eis prodidit? \'ut pati posset\', inquis, id est, ut ille optimus ignorantes adhuc in scelus mergeret. atquin et si dixisset, passurus esset. si dixero enim, inquit, uobis, non credetis. porro non credituri perseuerassent in necem eius. et cur non magis passurus esset, si alterius dei ac per hoc aduersarium creatoris (se) manifestasset? ergo non, ut pateretur, alium se tunc quoque supersedit ostendere, sed quoniam ex ore eius confessionem extorquere cupiebant, nec confesso tamen credituri, qui eum ex operibus scripturas adimplentibus agnouisse debuerant. ita eius fuit occultasse se, cui ultro debebatur agnitio. et tamen adhuc eis manum porrigens: abhinc, inquit, erit filius hominis sedens ad dexteram uirtutis dei. suggerebat enim se esse (de) Danihelis prophetia (filium hominis* et de psalmo Dauid (sedentem ad dexteram dei\'. itaque ex isto dicto et scripturae comparatione inluminati, quem se uellet intellegi: ergo, inquiunt, tu dei filius es? cuius dei, nisi quem solum nouerant? cuius dei, nisi quem in psalmo meminerant dixisse filio suo: sede ad dexteram meam? <sed respondit: uos dicitis, quasi: non ego\\ atquin confirmauit id se esse, quod illi dixerant, dum rursus interrogant. unde autem probabis interrogatiuo et non (et) ipsos confirmatiuo pronuntiasse: ergo tu filius dei es, ut, quia oblique ostenderat se per scripturas filium dei intellegendum, sic senserint: \'ergo tu dei es filius\', quod te non uis aperte dicere? atque ita et ille (uos dicitis\' confirmatiue respondit, et adeo sic fuit pronuntiatio eius, ut perseuerauerint in eo, quod pronuntiatio sapiebat.
thought_title: Woe to the One Who Betrays the Son of Man
pass_a_gloss: Woe, he says, to him through whom the Son of Man is betrayed. Therefore, now 'woe' is understood to be an exclamation of imprecation and commination, and it is attributed to one who is angry and offended, unless he who was about to relate such a great crime was playing innocently. But if innocently, 'woe' is empty; if not innocently, then he is certainly to be punished by him into whom the crime of betrayal was admitted. Furthermore, if knowingly he allowed the man, whom he himself had added to his company, to rush into such a great crime, do not now retract about the Creator concerning Adam what can be retorted against your own god: either he was ignorant, because he did not prevent the one who was about to sin, or he was unable to prevent, if he was not ignorant, or he did not wish to, if he both knew and was able, and thus he is to be judged malicious, who allowed his man to perish through fault. I advise, therefore, that you rather acknowledge the Creator in this also, and make him, who is the best God, contrary to your opinion. For even Peter, having spoken something presumptuously, shows a zealous God to you by destining it to denial. He ought to have been betrayed even with a kiss, the prophetic Christ, so that he, the Son, might be known, who was loved by the people with lips. Having been led into the council, he is asked if he himself is the Christ. About which Christ the Jews would have asked, unless about their own? Why, therefore, did he not betray another to them even then? 'So that he might suffer,' you say, that is, so that he might plunge the ignorant into crime. But even if he had said, he would have suffered. For if I say, he says, you will not believe. Furthermore, those who were not going to believe would have persevered in his death. And why was he not going to suffer even more, if he had manifested himself as another God and thus as an adversary of the Creator? Therefore, it was not so that he might suffer that he then also showed himself to be another, but because they wanted to extort a confession from his mouth, and yet, even if he had confessed, they would not have believed, who ought to have recognized him from the works fulfilling the scriptures. Thus, it was his to hide himself, to whom recognition was owed even spontaneously. And yet, still stretching out his hand to them: 'From now on,' he says, 'the Son of Man will be sitting at the right hand of the power of God.' For he was suggesting that he is the one from Daniel's prophecy, the Son of Man, and from David's psalm, sitting at the right hand of God. And so, from this saying and the comparison of scripture, they were enlightened, whom he wanted to be understood: 'Therefore, you are the Son of God?' Whose God, unless the one they alone knew? Whose God, unless the one they remembered saying to his Son in the psalm: 'Sit at my right hand?' But he responded: 'You say,' as if: 'not I.' But he confirmed that he is what they said, while they were asking again. Whence, however, will you prove that he spoke interrogatively and not also confirmatively: 'Therefore, you are the Son of God,' so that, because he had shown himself obliquely through the scriptures to be understood as the Son of God, they thus thought: 'Therefore, you are the Son of God,' which you do not want to say openly? And so, he also responded confirmatively with 'You say,' and thus his pronouncement was such that they persevered in what the pronouncement implied.
pass_b_english: "Woe to the man through whom the Son of Man is betrayed," he says. Therefore, the word "woe" must be understood as an outcry of imprecation and commination, attributed to someone who is angry and offended—unless the one who was about to recount such a monstrous crime was merely playing the innocent. But if he was playing the innocent, "woe" is an empty word; if not, then the man who admitted the crime of betrayal into himself must certainly be punished by the One he offended. Furthermore, if Jesus knowingly allowed the very man he had chosen for his company to plunge into such a crime, stop trying to score points against the Creator over Adam—those same arguments recoil on your own god. Either your god was ignorant, since he did not prevent the coming sinner; or he was unable to prevent it, if he was not ignorant; or he simply did not wish to, if he both knew and could—and in that case he must be judged malicious for letting his own man perish through fault. So I urge you: acknowledge the Creator here as well, and make him the one supreme God, contrary to your opinion. For even Peter, when he spoke presumptuously, shows you a zealous God by destining that boast for denial. Christ, the prophetic Christ, even had to be betrayed with a kiss—so that the Son, who was loved by the people with their lips, might be recognized. When he was dragged before the Sanhedrin, they asked whether he himself was the Christ. About which Christ would the Jews have inquired, if not their own? So why did he not hand over some other Messiah to them even then? "So that he could suffer," you say—that is, so that he could drag the ignorant into the crime. But even if he had named another, he still would have suffered. "For if I tell you," he says, "you will not believe" (Luke 22:67). And those who were not going to believe would have persisted in killing him anyway. And why would he not have suffered even more if he had revealed himself as a rival God and thus an adversary of the Creator? Therefore, it was not in order to suffer that he then also refrained from showing himself as another; it was because they wanted to extort a confession from his mouth. Yet even had he confessed, they would not have believed—though they ought to have recognized him from the works that fulfilled the Scriptures. So it fell to him to hide himself, though recognition was owed to him spontaneously. And still he held out his hand to them: "From now on the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God" (Luke 22:69). For he was signaling that he is the figure from Daniel's prophecy—the Son of Man (Dan 7:13)—and from David's psalm, the one seated at God's right hand (Ps 110:1). Enlightened by this saying and the comparison of Scripture, they grasped whom he wanted to be understood: "Are you then the Son of God?" Whose God, if not the only One they knew? Whose God, if not the One they remembered saying to his Son in the psalm, "Sit at my right hand"? He answered, "You say it," as if to say, "Not I." Yet he confirmed that he is exactly what they said, even as they kept pressing him. How, then, will you prove he spoke interrogatively rather than affirmatively—"You are the Son of God"—so that, because he had revealed himself obliquely through the Scriptures as the Son of God, they concluded, "Then you are the Son of God," which you refuse to say openly? And so he, too, answered affirmatively with "You say it"; indeed, his pronouncement was such that they persisted in the very claim his words implied.
